deals.headline: Visa heads to the Derby.
deals.summary: Visa is the Preferred Payment Partner of Churchill Downs and the 153rd Kentucky Derby in a multi-year deal the track calls first-of-its-kind.

article.standfirst: Visa has bought its way into the Kentucky Derby.
body: Churchill Downs has named Visa the Preferred Payment Partner of the racetrack and the 153rd Kentucky Derby, announced on Tuesday 20 October US time. The track's own release calls it a first-of-its-kind, multi-year partnership. It doesn't say how many years, and it doesn't put a dollar figure on it, so neither will we.

The pitch is about the punter at the gate. Visa clients and cardholders get exclusive Derby Weekend offers, experiences and better ways to buy. Churchill Downs says the deal should make ticket purchases more efficient and accessible. That is a payments company talking about the checkout, not just a logo on a rail.

Visa joins the track's existing Signature Partners, which the release lists as Woodford Reserve, Longines, Ford and SAP. That is a tight club: a bourbon, a watch brand, a carmaker and a software giant. Slotting a payments brand in alongside them says the Derby now sees the transaction itself as something worth selling.

The timing is clear too. The 153rd Derby runs on Saturday 1 May 2027, and the race carries a $5 million purse. Visa gets about six months to build activation before the roses are even on the shelf. Australians will know the company from its Rugby World Cup tie-up, so racing is another big, crowd-heavy property for it.

What to watch: whether the Derby Weekend offers reach cardholders outside the US, whether Churchill Downs adds more payments or ticketing partners around the tracks it runs, and what Visa builds for ticket buyers before May.
article.close: The Derby just got a new way to take your money.

article.standfirst: Hahn has landed the biggest pour of the Australian summer.
body: Tennis Australia has named Lion's Hahn the Official Beer of the Australian Open and the Australian Summer of Tennis in a multi-year deal announced on Thursday 22 October. Neither side has put a length or a number on it, so we won't either.

The centrepiece is Hahn House, a two-storey venue with a beer garden on Grand Slam Oval, which Tennis Australia is pitching as a new social hub for the tournament. Lion is bringing more of its portfolio too: Stone & Wood takes over Garden Square, and Four Pillars runs a new gin bar at Kia Arena.

Away from Melbourne Park, Hahn plans limited-edition packaging, competitions, tennis merch and surprise experiences, plus pop-up pickleball courts and racket-shaped drinks trays around the country. That reach matters. The AO is a fortnight, but the Summer of Tennis gives Hahn a whole season of pub and bottle-shop activity to hang it on.

It also rounds out a big sporting slate for the brand. Hahn already holds the naming rights to the Hahn Australia Cup and is the official beer of the Wallabies, so the AO gives Lion a marquee summer property to sit alongside its football and rugby plays.
What to watch: how Hahn House lands with AO crowds in January, and whether Lion stacks more of its brands across the Summer of Tennis events outside Melbourne.

deals.headline: Woolworths stocks up on rugby.
deals.summary: Woolworths is the Official Supermarket Supporter of the men's Rugby World Cup 2027 and women's Rugby World Cup 2029, both in Australia.

article.standfirst: Woolworths has put its hand up for both home Rugby World Cups.
body: Woolworths has been named the Official Supermarket Supporter of the men's Rugby World Cup 2027 and the women's Rugby World Cup 2029, both being played in Australia. The deal was announced on Tuesday 20 October. Neither side has put a number or an end date on it beyond the two tournaments, so we won't either.

It slots Woolworths into World Rugby's Official Suppliers and Supporters tier, alongside names like Dove Men+Care, Gilbert, Macron and Mitsubishi Estate. Above that sit the official partners (Liqui Moly, Coca-Cola, IHG) and the principal partners, Emirates, Asahi Super Dry and Visa.

The interesting bit is the retail media angle. Woolworths says its Cartology network will open up brand opportunities around the tournaments. That turns a supermarket sponsorship into something bigger: a channel other brands can buy into, with the World Cup as the hook and the checkout as the payoff. Woolworths reckons it serves around 24 million customers a week, which is a lot of eyeballs for a pack of snags or a slab of something cold.

The men's tournament runs from 1 October to 13 November 2027, with 24 teams across seven host cities. Woolworths is pitching itself as a one-stop shop for fans on both sides of the Tasman, with fans in New Zealand part of the pitch as much as fans here.
What to watch: how hard Woolworths pushes Cartology deals off the back of this, and whether the other big grocers or liquor chains try to muscle in around the edges with their own rugby plays.
article.close: In a home World Cup, the supermarket aisle might be the best seat in the house.

deals.headline: IREN lands at the Bernabéu.
deals.summary: Sydney-founded AI cloud provider IREN is Real Madrid's new official sponsor, reported as the club's official AI cloud partner.

article.standfirst: A Sydney-founded AI cloud company has just put its name next to the biggest badge in club football.
body: Real Madrid named IREN as a new official sponsor on Sunday 18 October. Trade coverage from Sportcal and Footy Headlines has IREN billed as the club's official AI cloud partner. Neither side has said how long the deal runs or what it's worth, so we won't guess.

If the name rings a bell, it should. IREN started out in Sydney, is listed on the Nasdaq and now runs as an AI cloud and data centre business. In June it signed a multi-year deal to put its badge on Golden State Warriors jerseys from the 2026-27 season, a patch reportedly worth more than US$50 million a year and reportedly the richest sponsorship in North American team sport.

The Madrid deal makes more sense once you look at where IREN is building. In June it completed the purchase of Spanish data centre developer Nostrum Group, picking up around 490 megawatts of secured power in Spain. So this isn't just a logo on a stadium screen. IREN is buying awareness in a country where it's putting real infrastructure in the ground, and doing it with the one club everyone in Spain, and most of the planet, knows.

For the category, this is the AI infrastructure money finally reaching European football's top table. Crypto and fintech brands bought their way into sport on hype. The compute crowd has hard assets, big customers and a reason to be known by governments, landlords and talent as much as by fans. Expect them to keep paying for the biggest badges they can find.

What to watch: whether IREN's role grows into matchday branding or technology work at the Bernabéu, and whether the Warriors and Real Madrid become a template for more AI cloud firms chasing global clubs.
article.close: AI cloud money has found the biggest stage in club football, and it won't be the last.

deals.headline: GWM rolls into Parra.
deals.summary: Multi-year deal makes GWM the Eels' official automotive partner from 2027, with its logo on the sleeve of both the NRL and NRLW playing jerseys.

article.standfirst: GWM wants to be Australia's number five car brand, and it's driving through Parramatta to get there.
body: The Parramatta Eels have signed GWM as their official automotive partner on a multi-year deal that kicks off in the 2027 season. The car maker also takes the sleeve on both the NRL and NRLW playing jerseys, so the same badge runs across the men's and women's programs. Neither side has put a number on it.

It's been a big week in the Eels' commercial office. Two days earlier the club confirmed adidas as its new apparel partner across the NRL and NRLW sides, with the new kit due in Round 1 next year. So by the time Parra runs out in 2027 the jersey, and what's printed on the arm, will both be new.

For GWM this is part of a pattern. It's already the official automotive partner of the NZ Warriors and a joint major partner at Richmond in the AFL. GWM's Australia and New Zealand chief operating officer John Kett was blunt about the goal: become the country's number five automotive brand. He also had a crack at the club's ambitions, saying that for Parramatta the goal is premiership number five.

The logic is easy to follow. New South Wales is the biggest car market in the country and western Sydney is a heartland of rugby league, so a sleeve at Parra puts the brand in front of a huge chunk of potential buyers every week. Taking the asset across both the NRL and NRLW kits also squeezes more airtime out of one spot on the shirt, and gives GWM a presence in the women's game without a separate deal.

What to watch next: how GWM activates it. Car brands in footy usually lean on vehicle fleets, member offers and dealer tie-ins, so expect GWM to show up well beyond the sleeve. The other thing to watch is whether GWM keeps adding clubs. Two codes and three big teams in, it's starting to look like a portfolio rather than a one-off.
article.close: New kit, new car partner, same week. Not a bad start to 2027 for the Eels.

article.standfirst: adidas is putting the Parramatta Eels in three stripes.
body: The Parramatta Eels have signed a multi-year deal that makes adidas the club's official apparel partner. It covers a lot of ground: the NRL and NRLW teams, the club's elite academy programs and its junior representative sides. Both top teams will run out in adidas for the first time in Round 1 of the 2027 season. Neither side has put out a length or a dollar figure.

The club launched it with a campaign called "Made for Parra", and the kit and retail range are due to be unveiled at a launch later this year. That reveal is where the fans get their first proper look at what three stripes in blue and gold actually means.

Why it matters: apparel is one of the few deals that touches every part of a club. Sponsors get a logo on a jersey. A kit supplier gets the jersey itself, the training gear, the merch store and every junior player pulling on a Parra top on a Saturday morning. Signing the pathways as well as first grade means adidas is in front of the next generation of Eels fans years before they buy a membership.

It's also a nice get for adidas, a brand most Aussie fans link with football and rugby union rather than the NRL. Landing the Eels in Western Sydney, with a deal that runs right down to the juniors, gives it a real foothold in rugby league heartland.
What to watch next: the kit reveal and how hard adidas pushes the retail side, and whether the brand follows up with more rugby league clubs once the Eels range is on the shelves.

deals.headline: Monaco's shirt for Europe.
deals.summary: Monaco insurance broker takes the front of the shirt for AS Monaco's Conference League games this season, plus LED boards at Stade Louis-II.

article.standfirst: Monaco has signed a shirt sponsor just for its European nights.
body: AS Monaco has named Suisscourtage Assurances its new major partner for the UEFA Conference League. The insurance broker's name goes on the front of the first-team shirt for European matches this season, and it picks up LED advertising at home games at Stade Louis-II. No fee or length beyond the coming season has been put out. The campaign starts away to CSKA Sofia on Thursday 15 October.

It's a local deal through and through. Suisscourtage was founded in Monaco in 1988, sits inside the JV Pastor Group and employs 220 people, working with private clients and businesses that need cover for complex risks and high-value assets. Monaco CEO Thiago Scuro pitched it as two Monegasque organisations joining forces, and that's the point: a club from a tiny principality putting a home-grown business on the shirt when it travels.

The timing tells the story. Only last week Monaco signed Mammouth AI as a premium partner through 2029, with the AI company appearing on the shirt in Ligue 1. This is Monaco's first go at the Conference League, so rather than bundle Europe into an existing deal, the club treated it as fresh inventory and sold it separately.

That's the bit worth watching across the game. Competition-specific shirt deals let clubs squeeze more out of the same piece of fabric, and they open the door to brands that can't stretch to a full-season domestic deal but can afford a European run. For a broker chasing wealthy clients, a handful of televised European nights with a club tied to Monaco is a tidy fit.

What to watch next: how far Monaco go in the competition, because a deeper run means more matches and more value for Suisscourtage, and whether the deal rolls over if Monaco land back in the Champions League.
article.close: Expect more clubs to sell the shirt one competition at a time.

deals.headline: Adobe serves up AI.
deals.summary: Multi-year deal as Official AI Marketing and Creativity Partner. Adobe's first tennis sponsorship worldwide.

article.standfirst: Adobe just signed its first tennis sponsorship anywhere in the world, and it picked the Australian Open.
body: Tennis Australia has named Adobe the Official AI Marketing and Creativity Partner of the Australian Open in a multi-year deal that will roll out in phases. Neither side has put a number or an end date on it. What they have spelled out is the job: Tennis Australia will run Adobe CX Enterprise across its digital setup to get a sharper read on what fans actually want, then use that to steer them to the right match, somewhere to eat or a bit of entertainment at Melbourne Park, and to tailor its comms market by market.

It's a big first for Adobe. The software giant has never backed tennis before, so the AO becomes its entry point into the sport globally. That's a handy feather in Tennis Australia's cap, which keeps pitching the AO as the Grand Slam of Asia-Pacific and wants partners who can help it reach that regional audience.

The interesting bit is how the value flows. Plenty of tech partnerships in sport stop at a logo on the court and a line in the release. This one only works if the product is actually used, and used well. Tennis Australia gets enterprise tools to personalise at a scale it couldn't build itself, and Adobe gets a two-week global shop window every January to show its AI doing something useful for real people. Fans also get AI creative tools to make their own content, which ticks the engagement box and feeds more first-party data back into the system.

The brief runs well past the tournament too. Both sides say the aim is year-round participation across Australia and the wider Asia-Pacific, which puts the deal squarely in the business of growing the game for the other fifty weeks of the year.

What to watch: how much of this fans actually notice at AO 2027. If the personalisation lands and the creative tools get used, expect other rights holders to start writing data and martech into their partner briefs rather than just selling space.
article.close: The AO has long called itself the Grand Slam of Asia-Pacific. Now it's got the martech to back that up.

Football's commercial ceiling keeps rising because categories with nothing to do with the pitch (beauty, fashion, lifestyle) want a piece of the audience and content machine big clubs now run. PSG's off-pitch program is built for exactly this kind of crossover.
A beauty major choosing football over tennis or F1, where cosmetics brands usually sit, says the audience around the men's game has gotten too big to ignore.
article.close: Expect more unlikely categories to follow L'Oréal into football before this cycle is out.

deals.headline: MILO goes to the NBA.
deals.summary: Multi-year deal across 21 markets including Australia and New Zealand, from January 2027.

article.standfirst: MILO just became an official NBA partner.
body: Nestlé has signed a multi-year global marketing partnership with the NBA, covering 21 markets including Australia and New Zealand. MILO, Nescau and Nesquik all become Official Partners, with activations across Jr. NBA programs, NBA Global Games and NBA House starting from January 2027.

A brand this tied to junior cricket here is now putting the same weight behind basketball, and doing it across 21 countries in one deal rather than market by market. That's rights holders bundling scale the way streaming platforms bundle territories.
It also says basketball has earned a seat at the table alongside the sports MILO has backed at grassroots level for decades.
article.close: Expect MILO to lean hard on that grassroots playbook once the Aussie and Kiwi activations land.

deals.summary: Major Partner and Official Sneaker Supplier to the Kiwis, Kiwi Ferns and Wheelchair Kiwis.

article.standfirst: JD Sports just signed its first-ever national rugby league deal, and chose New Zealand Rugby League to do it.
body: JD becomes Major Partner and Official Sneaker Supplier to the Kiwis, Kiwi Ferns and Wheelchair Kiwis ahead of the Rugby League World Cup, with exclusive playing-day product and content tied to the tournament.

Sneaker brands have mostly chased football, basketball and the NBA/NFL orbit. A first national rugby league deal says the category now sees real commercial upside in the code, with the World Cup's global stage probably doing the heavy lifting.
Expect other footwear brands to take notice.
article.close: Rugby league might be about to become footwear's next battleground.

article.standfirst: Visa just ended thirty years of league-wide NFL sponsorship to bet on individual teams instead.
body: The blanket partnership, running since 1995, lapsed and wasn't renewed. Visa replaced it with 13 separate team deals: seven brand new, four long-term renewals and two already in place. The renewals cover the Buffalo Bills, New England Patriots, Pittsburgh Steelers and San Francisco 49ers, while the new signings include the Dallas Cowboys, Kansas City Chiefs and Philadelphia Eagles.

A league logo buys visibility everywhere and control nowhere. Thirteen team deals buy Visa a say in which markets get which activations, plus fan data a blanket deal never handed over, and a clearer read on return in each market.
Other blue-chip league sponsors, from banking to airlines and insurance, will be asking the same question before their next renewal.
article.close: Thirty years as one NFL deal just became thirteen. Worth watching who copies the model next.

article.standfirst: Bridgestone is walking back into top-flight motorsport, this time as both tyre supplier and title sponsor.
body: The Japanese giant has signed on as Formula E's sole tyre supplier from the 2026/27 season, taking title billing on four marquee rounds including Mexico City and Tokyo. The new tyres are built from 65% recycled and renewable material, launching alongside the championship's next-gen GEN4 car.

A legacy tyre brand betting big on electric racing says plenty about where motorsport sponsorship money is heading. Pairing the comeback with a real sustainability figure, rather than just a logo on the sidewall, gives Bridgestone a story to tell well beyond the deal itself.
article.close: Expect more legacy automotive brands chasing the same electric-racing halo in seasons to come.

article.standfirst: Rice Stadium has stood for 76 years without a sponsor's name on it. Until now.
body: First Community Credit Union has signed a 20-year naming rights deal, renaming the venue First Community Stadium and helping fund Rice University's $120 million Gateway Project renovation. It's the stadium's first-ever naming rights deal, and it kicked in for Rice's home game against UTSA.

Credit unions buying into college sports isn't new, but tying the deal directly to stadium financing is sharper. It turns sponsorship into a funding tool for schools without a billion-dollar athletics budget.
Expect more mid-major programs to chase this model instead of waiting on state money.
article.close: Naming rights used to be for the big programs. Not anymore.

article.standfirst: An NRL franchise that won't play its first match for two years just landed Coca-Cola as a premier partner.
body: Coca-Cola Europacific Partners PNG has signed on as premier partner of the PNG Chiefs, the NRL's new Papua New Guinea franchise debuting in 2028. The deal includes exclusive jersey sleeve branding and exclusive non-alcoholic beverage rights across matchdays and hospitality.

Rugby league is close to a national obsession in Papua New Guinea, and brands have eyed it for years as a market the NRL couldn't ignore. A beverage giant backing the team before it's played a game signals confidence that passion converts into commercial value, not just expansion goodwill.
article.close: Expect more brands to treat PNG's NRL entry as a market play, not a novelty.

article.standfirst: Bloom Energy just signed the second-biggest jersey patch deal in NBA history, and this one's coming from the energy sector.
body: The Philadelphia 76ers have named the fuel-cell energy company their new patch partner, replacing Crypto.com, in a multi-year deal that also covers the Delaware Blue Coats, with a seven-figure community investment attached. It lands as LeBron James's arrival spikes ticket and merchandise demand in Philadelphia.

Energy infrastructure money is chasing NBA real estate the way crypto and fintech did a few years back. Golden State carries IREN, and Philadelphia has now picked up the sector's second-biggest cheque. Basketball's reach is being priced at AI-boom rates, before AI itself has any real link to the sport.
article.close: Expect more energy and AI infrastructure names on NBA jerseys before the season's out.

deals.headline: Mascots get NIL deals.
deals.summary: First-of-its-kind mascot NIL deal via Learfield. Touchdowns trigger shelter cat meals.

article.standfirst: Six college mascots have NIL deals now, and every touchdown their team scores earns a shelter cat a meal.
body: Friskies has signed what's being called a first-of-its-kind NIL deal with six university mascots, including Truman the Tiger (Missouri), Aubie (Auburn) and Cosmo (BYU), brokered through Learfield. Scoring plays this season trigger donated meals for cats in shelters.
Mascots have sat on the fringe of the NIL boom since it opened beyond athletes, and this is the most creative use of it yet: a real in-game trigger instead of a logo on a costume.
It's cheap, carries almost no scandal risk, and gives brands a lane into college sports that doesn't compete with athletes for NIL money.
article.close: Expect more brands chasing mascots next, not quarterbacks.

deals.headline: Equity in her own tee.
deals.summary: First signature kicking tee in women's rugby, with 20% of every sale to de Goede.

article.standfirst: A New Zealand kicking-tee brand just gave a Canadian rugby captain equity in her own gear.
body: Rugby Bricks has signed World Player of the Year Sophie de Goede for the first signature kicking tee in women's rugby. The RB Vortex is co-designed by de Goede, with a red colourway for her Canadian heritage, and she takes 20% of every unit sold.

Signature product deals with revenue share are common in men's sport (boots, bats, rackets) but rare in women's rugby, where sponsorship infrastructure is still catching up. A boutique brand backing a genuine star with real upside, rather than chasing a marquee logo deal, builds credibility fast.
article.close: More equipment brands will start trading flat fees for equity in the athletes wearing their gear.

article.standfirst: An AI infrastructure company just bought naming rights to a Power Four football stadium.
body: Databricks has locked in a deal worth up to US$22.8M for naming rights to Cal's Memorial Stadium field, now Databricks Field, plus helmet branding through the 2026 season. It's a homecoming of sorts: the company was founded out of UC Berkeley.

College stadium naming rights used to be insurance companies and regional banks. Now it's AI infrastructure players with the deepest pockets in tech, buying brand equity with a young, technical audience and the alumni base that built them.
article.close: Expect more AI money to show up on stadiums before it shows up on jerseys.

deals.summary: Exclusive global licence for real-money La Liga games outside Spain.

article.standfirst: La Liga has just become a real-money gambling operator.
body: Spain's top football league has signed an exclusive global licensing deal with B2B studio LIGAS Gaming, letting it build and distribute real-money football games under the La Liga brand across regulated markets outside Spain.

That's a real shift in how a league makes money from gambling. Rather than collecting ad dollars from a betting sponsor, La Liga now earns directly off every wager placed inside its own branded product.
With betting-ad rules tightening across multiple markets, licensing the IP directly lets a rights holder keep the upside while sidestepping some of that scrutiny.
article.close: Expect more leagues to start treating real-money gaming as a product they own outright, not just an ad category they sell into.

article.standfirst: A US sandwich chain just bought naming rights to an English football trophy.
body: Jersey Mike's is the new title sponsor of the EFL Trophy, now renamed the Jersey Mike's Trophy, in a five-year deal worth around £5 million, the most lucrative commercial deal in the competition's history. It covers League One, League Two and invited academy sides, and lands alongside Jersey Mike's push into the UK and Ireland, where it's targeting up to 400 new stores.
Going in through a lower-tier cup rather than a Premier League shirt is a cheaper way to buy visibility while a brand is still opening stores, long before it needs top-flight prices to get noticed.
article.close: Expect more US challenger brands to use the undercard to get a foothold in English football before they ever go near the main event.

deals.headline: Mbappé takes equity.
deals.summary: Leaves Nike after 20 years, taking equity instead of a standard fee.

article.standfirst: Kylian Mbappé just walked away from Nike after 20 years, and picked equity over a bigger cheque.
body: He's signed with Swiss brand On, taking equity in the business instead of a standard endorsement fee. On will build its first football boots in 2027, and has already added Thierry Henry as director of football.

The equity angle matters more than the boots. On is betting that owning part of a challenger brand beats another decade of royalty cheques from the market leader, and Mbappé's happy to bet alongside them. Federer proved the model works in tennis, and On is running the same play in football.
Expect more superstars to ask for equity over a signing bonus.
article.close: Boot deals used to be about who pays the most. Now the smart ones are about who owns the most.

article.standfirst: McLaren Racing just signed a kitchen appliance brand as an official partner, and the deal goes well past logos on the car.
body: SharkNinja is now a multi-year partner across McLaren's Formula 1, Arrow McLaren IndyCar, Hypercar and F1 ACADEMY programmes. The deal folds SharkNinja into the team's Racing Accelerator Programme, giving the appliance maker access to McLaren's engineering process for product development, not just trackside branding.

Motorsport sponsorship has traditionally sold speed and glamour. This one sells R&D access. When a consumer brand buys into a race team's engineering process rather than a grid slot, sponsorship starts looking more like a product partnership than a media buy, and that's a much harder asset for a rival to copy than a logo.
article.close: Expect more tech and consumer brands chasing access over airtime.

article.standfirst: Firmus Technologies just put its name on Cricket Tasmania's playing shirts.
body: The Australian AI infrastructure company has signed a five-year deal as principal partner of the Hobart Hurricanes and major partner of the Tasmanian Tigers, across both BBL and WBBL. Over $1 million of it goes straight into grassroots cricket through a new program called Beyond Boundaries.

AI and data infrastructure firms are cashed up right now, but most of that spend goes on compute rather than brand building. Front-of-shirt space on a regional cricket team is a fast way to buy mainstream trust outside the tech press, and tying it to grassroots funding makes the deal harder to dismiss as a vanity buy.
article.close: More AI infrastructure names on sporting shirts feels inevitable from here.

article.standfirst: adidas just bought naming rights to the academy that produced Bernardo Silva, João Félix and Rúben Dias.
body: adidas has extended its kit deal with Benfica through 2033, reported at €120 million and the biggest sponsorship in Portuguese football history. It stretches a relationship that goes back to 1997, and the new terms hand adidas naming rights to Benfica's Seixal training academy, which becomes the adidas Benfica Campus.

Kit deals usually buy visibility on match day. This one buys adidas a permanent presence inside the pipeline that actually produces the players, turning a facility into brand real estate instead of just matchday exposure.
Once every major stadium already has a naming partner, training grounds look like the next thing clubs can sell.
article.close: Sponsorship money is starting to chase where players are made, not just where they're worn.

article.standfirst: Sunderland just became the 11th Premier League club this season to sign a shirt sponsor that isn't licensed to operate in the UK.
body: Sunderland have signed Shuffle, a crypto casino platform licensed only in Curaçao, as sleeve sponsor across the Premier League, domestic cups and the UEFA Europa League. The multi-year deal replaces previous sponsor Serios Group and debuted on the shirt against Arsenal.

Front-of-shirt gambling ads are now banned in the Premier League, and sleeves have become the workaround. Unlicensed operators are filling that gap faster than regulators can close it, with a government consultation on banning them unlikely to bite before 2027/28. Entain has been writing to rival clubs urging them to cut ties, yet eleven clubs now carry unlicensed brands anyway.
article.close: The front of the shirt is regulated. The sleeve, for now, isn't.

article.standfirst: Liverpool just ended a 17-year sponsorship to sign one that pays more than double.
body: Liverpool have named Turkish Airlines as their new front-of-shirt sponsor from 2027, replacing Standard Chartered after 17 years. The five-year deal is reported at roughly £60 million a year, close to £300 million in total and the biggest shirt sponsorship in football history.

Standard Chartered's deal was one of the longest-running in the Premier League. Walking away from that kind of continuity for this kind of number shows how far shirt values have moved. Airlines have circled football's biggest shirts for years (Emirates, Qatar Airways), and Turkish Airlines just set a new price for the privilege.
article.close: Expect the next round of Premier League shirt renewals to be priced off this deal, not the one it replaced.

article.standfirst: Starbucks just put its name on a football shirt for the first time anywhere in the world.
body: The coffee giant has signed as an official partner of Ligue 1 side Toulouse FC. It's Starbucks' first-ever club shirt sponsorship in football, after years of stadium and event tie-ins but never a jersey.

Going with a mid-table Ligue 1 club rather than a Premier League giant looks like a deliberate test run. Toulouse gets a genuinely global brand on the shirt, and Starbucks gets to trial football sponsorship at a fraction of the cost of a top-league deal.
article.close: Watch for Starbucks to move up market fast if the Toulouse deal lands well.

Most jersey-patch deals stay locked to the marquee sport, where the cameras are. Buying across an entire athletic department trades spotlight exposure for blanket presence: every roster, and every recruiting pitch the school makes.
article.close: Expect more brands to buy the whole department instead of just the biggest sport.

article.standfirst: Kayo just bought the broadcast rights to a surfing league that doesn't launch until 2028.
body: Kayo Sports and BINGE have locked in exclusive rights to the new Surfing Super League, a franchise-based comp built on a fixed, LIV Golf-style format: eight weeks, set weekend timeslots and 50 hours of coverage. The deal was signed 17 months before a single heat gets surfed.

This is a format bet. Kayo is backing a made-for-TV competition more than a year out from its first heat, with no existing tour or star roster to lean on yet. Surf has always fought its broadcast window, and a fixed format designed for TV from day one might be the fix the traditional tour never found.
article.close: Expect more sports to build the broadcast deal first and the competition second.
